summary: Describes how SNMPv1, SNMPv2, and SNMPv3 can coexist, and how to convert between the information definitions of the older frameworks and the newer ones. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Three versions of a network management language are in use. This memo explains how they can live together and how to translate between them.

subtitle: How SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and SNMPv3 devices share one network, and how to convert old MIB modules to the newer format.

tldr.problem: Networks ended up with devices speaking three versions of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework (SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and SNMPv3), each with different data definitions, error codes and notification formats.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives rules for converting MIB modules from SMIv1 to SMIv2, for translating notification parameters, for multi-lingual agents and proxies that map between versions, and defines the SNMP-COMMUNITY-MIB that ties community strings into the SNMPv3 architecture.
tldr.outcome: Old and new managers and agents can interoperate, though a proxy that translates SNMPv3 down to SNMPv1 loses authentication and privacy, and the RFC recommends deploying SNMPv3 instead of earlier versions.

today: RFC 3584 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 74) that obsoletes RFC 2576, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It still recommends SNMPv3 over earlier versions.

sections.title: Three Frameworks, One Network
sections.content:
RFC 3584 describes coexistence between SNMPv3, SNMPv2 and the original SNMPv1 frameworks. It covers four things: converting MIB documents between SMIv1 and SMIv2 formats, mapping notification parameters, approaches to coexistence in a "multi-lingual" network (including proxies), and the SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c message processing and community-based security models that adapt older versions to the View-Based Access Control Model (VACM).

SNMPv1 is defined by RFC 1157 (the protocol), RFC 1155 and RFC 1212 (the SMIv1 way of describing objects) and RFC 1215 (traps). SNMPv2 uses SMIv2 (RFCs 2578, 2579 and 2580) plus the protocol operations, transport mappings and base MIB of RFCs 3416, 3417 and 3418. SNMPv2c, from RFC 1901, wraps SNMPv2 PDUs in a community-based message. SNMPv3 is defined by RFCs 3411 to 3415 and reuses the SNMPv2 definitions, so text about SNMPv2 PDU types and operations applies to both SNMPv2c and SNMPv3.
sections.eli5: There are three versions of one network-watching language. This memo explains how devices that speak different versions can still work together.

sections.title: Converting MIB Modules from SMIv1 to SMIv2
sections.content:
SMIv2 is nearly a proper superset of SMIv1, so SMIv1 MIB modules can still be used with protocol versions that carry SNMPv2 PDUs. To make a module actually conform to SMIv2, a list of changes is required. Among them: the IMPORTS must reference SNMPv2-SMI, the MODULE-IDENTITY macro must follow immediately, Counter becomes Counter32, Gauge becomes Gauge32 (or Unsigned32), and ACCESS becomes MAX-ACCESS. Objects with status mandatory or optional must be changed to current, deprecated or obsolete, and related objects must be collected into OBJECT-GROUPs.

Conversion does not by itself require deprecating objects. A NetworkAddress in an INDEX needs a new not-accessible INTEGER index object whose value is always 1, placed just before it, so the converted module still works with SNMPv1 agents and managers. Optional improvements include adding UNITS clauses and bounds on unconstrained integers and strings.

Traps convert too: each TRAP-TYPE becomes a NOTIFICATION-TYPE, the ENTERPRISE clause is removed, VARIABLES is renamed OBJECTS, and a STATUS and DESCRIPTION are added. Standards-track modules also need MODULE-COMPLIANCE statements, and RFC 1303 capability statements become AGENT-CAPABILITIES.
sections.eli5: An old recipe card has to be rewritten on the new card format. Some boxes get renamed and some new boxes must be filled in, but the dish is the same.

sections.title: Translating Notification Parameters
sections.content:
SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 describe a notification differently. SNMPv1 notification parameters are enterprise, agent-addr, generic-trap, specific-trap, time-stamp and a list of variable-bindings. SNMPv2 parameters are sysUpTime, snmpTrapOID and a variable-binding list. Translation is needed when an entity must send a notification in a version other than the one it generated, and when a proxy forwards a notification across versions. It does not matter whether the notification is a trap or an inform.

Going from SNMPv1 to SNMPv2, sysUpTime is taken from the time-stamp. If generic-trap is enterpriseSpecific(6), the snmpTrapOID is the enterprise value followed by 0 and the specific-trap value. Otherwise it is the matching standard trap from RFC 3418. When a proxy does the translation it also appends snmpTrapAddress.0, snmpTrapCommunity.0 and snmpTrapEnterprise.0 bindings so the original agent address, community string and enterprise survive.

Going the other way, the generic-trap value is set from the standard trap OID, or to 6 for anything else, and the specific-trap is the last sub-identifier of the snmpTrapOID (zero for standard traps). If the SNMPv2 bindings contain a Counter64 object, the translation cannot be done and the notification cannot be sent using SNMPv1.
sections.eli5: It is like translating a postcard from one language to another. The important facts are copied across, and if a word has no match in the old language, the card cannot be sent that way.

sections.title: Multi-lingual Agents and Managers
sections.content:
A multi-lingual implementation supports several message versions, typically SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3, so it can talk to any single-version peer. A command generator picks a version for each request, for instance from a local database. When it picks SNMPv1 it MUST downgrade a GetBulk request to GetNext, ignoring the non-repeaters and max-repetitions values and setting error-status and error-index to zero.

A command responder that uses SNMPv2 access to MIB data while handling an SNMPv1 message must hide what SNMPv1 cannot express. It MUST NOT return a Counter64 value in an SNMPv1 response; such objects are treated as not in view, so a GetRequest for one gets noSuchName and a GetNextRequest skips over them. SNMPv2 exceptions (noSuchObject, noSuchInstance, endOfMibView) are converted to noSuchName, with the error-index pointing at the offending binding and the original binding list returned.

A notification originator translates parameters to match the configured version, and when it sends with SNMPv1 the PDU is always a Trap, whether the notification type is trap or inform. A notification receiver has no special requirements.
sections.eli5: A helper who speaks both old and new dialects talks to each friend in the friend's dialect. If the old dialect has no word for something, the helper says "no such thing" instead of using a word the friend cannot understand.

sections.title: Proxy Translation Between Versions
sections.content:
A proxy forwarder lets entities that each speak only one, different, version communicate. In cases not listed in the RFC, it forwards a PDU unchanged. The upstream version is the one used between the command generator (or notification receiver) and the proxy; the downstream version is the one used between the proxy and the command responder (or notification originator).

When upstream is newer than downstream, a GetBulkRequest forwarded over SNMPv1 is treated as having non-repeaters and max-repetitions of 0 and sent as a GetNextRequest. A tooBig response gets special care: the proxy empties the variable-bindings, and for an original GetBulk it retries once with only the first binding, because retrying many times is deemed too expensive. A received Trap is translated and forwarded as an SNMPv2-Trap.

When upstream is older, a response containing Counter64 or an exception makes the proxy build a noSuchName response. For GetNext, the proxy must re-send the request, substituting the names of any Counter64 bindings, until none are returned. An InformRequest can only be forwarded over SNMPv2c or SNMPv3, so SNMPv1 forwarding configuration for it is ignored.
sections.eli5: A proxy is like a translator standing between two people who share no language. It repeats each message in the other person's language, and sometimes has to ask again if the answer was too long.

sections.title: Mapping Error Codes
sections.content:
The five SNMPv1 error-status values (noError, tooBig, noSuchName, badValue, genErr) map to themselves in SNMPv2. SNMPv2 has many more, and they are folded into the SNMPv1 set when a response goes to an SNMPv1 peer: value-related errors become badValue, access and naming errors become noSuchName, and resource or commit failures become genErr.

One mapping has a side effect. Whenever the SNMPv2 authorizationError is translated to noSuchName, the counter snmpInBadCommunityUses MUST be incremented. SNMPv1 error codes SHOULD NOT be used unchanged for SNMPv2c or SNMPv3 messages, except in proxy forwarding.
sections.eli5: The new language has lots of ways to say "that did not work". The old language only has five, so the translator picks the closest one.

sections.title: Community Strings and the SNMP-COMMUNITY-MIB
sections.content:
To fit SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c into the SNMP architecture, the RFC defines the SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c Message Processing Models and Community-Based Security Models. The SnmpMessageProcessingModel value is 0 for SNMPv1 and 1 for SNMPv2c; the security model value is 1 or 2. The security level is always noAuthNoPriv.

The SNMP-COMMUNITY-MIB maps a community name to a securityName, contextEngineID and contextName, and the other way round. On an incoming request, the model searches the snmpCommunityTable in lexicographic order and picks the first row whose community name matches (and whose transport tag, if not empty, matches the source address). If none matches, an authentication failure occurs and snmpInBadCommunityNames is incremented. This lets VACM limit what even unsecured SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c requests can reach.

The MIB also augments snmpTargetAddrTable with snmpTargetAddrTMask, a bit mask that lets one entry match a whole subnet, and snmpTargetAddrMMS, a maximum message size. These extra values are used only where the text says so.
sections.eli5: A community string is like a club password. This MIB is the club's list that says what each password lets you look at, so even the old, unlocked version can be given limits.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 provide no security themselves, but mapping community names into securityName and contextName allows view-based access control to restrict them, and administrators should use that to avoid unauthorized access to MIB data. A proxy that forwards an authenticated, encrypted SNMPv3 message over SNMPv1 loses that protection, so proxies need careful configuration, perhaps with an encrypted tunnel.

The snmpCommunityTable allows creation and deletion of community strings, a potentially serious hole, so write access should be restricted, preferably to SNMPv3 with VACM and USM using authentication and privacy. Reading it can expose community strings that give more access than the usual public one.

The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with cryptographic security and says that deploying versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The old versions leave the door unlocked. Put guards on the community list, and when you can, use the newest version, which has real locks.
